title: We're building an adaptive prediction engine. Could the same approach improve algorithmic trading?
author: Rare_Reference3909
selftext:
Hi everyone,

We're developing Nexyria, an independent quantitative
intelligence project focused on forecasting, market
analysis and evidence-based decision systems.

One of our research projects is APEX, an adaptive
prediction engine.

The idea behind APEX is relatively simple:

Instead of assuming that one forecasting method
works best in every situation, we investigate
whether a system can identify the current data
environment and select an appropriate method.

We've started testing this approach on business
forecasting datasets.

Some early results:

• APEX Business V0.1 improved RMSLE by approximately
  1.13% over its baseline in an external Kaggle
  evaluation.

• APEX Business V0.2 was evaluated on 1,885 daily
  observations from the Walmart M5 dataset.

• In that second evaluation, APEX matched the
  strongest baseline but did not outperform it.

• The result was classified as MIXED under our
  predefined validation protocol.

This second result was particularly interesting.

APEX selected the same forecasting method across
all 1,885 observations.

It performed reasonably well, but it did not
demonstrate meaningful adaptive behavior.

That raises an important research question:

How can we distinguish genuine adaptation
from a selector that simply learns to favor
one strong baseline?

We're now considering whether this research
approach could eventually be useful in our
separate algorithmic trading system,
Nexyria Trader.

For example:

Could an adaptive selector help identify
different market regimes?

Could it determine when certain trading
strategies are more appropriate?

Could it identify environments where
the safest decision is not to trade?

We haven't validated APEX for trading,
and we're not claiming that it improves
trading performance.

Our intention would be to research it
offline first, using historical data,
walk-forward testing and forward validation,
before considering any integration.

I'm interested in hearing from people
working on adaptive systems, regime detection
or quantitative strategy selection.

What approaches have you found most useful
for distinguishing real adaptive improvements
from overfitting?

And what validation methods would you
consider essential before trusting such
a selector in a live trading environment?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
in markets the regime detector overfits first, since it's tuned on the same history it's meant to classify. freeze the switch at last year's settings and see how much of the edge survives.

for the rule-testing half on US shares, Quantradin, a tester I built, grades a rule with no future bars and runs whatever holds up on paper. quantradin.com

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That's a very good point, and it's exactly one
of the risks we're trying to address.

Our approach is to freeze the selector and its
decision rules before evaluating them on unseen data.

We've already seen why this matters in our
forecasting research: one version matched the
strongest baseline across 1,885 observations,
but failed to demonstrate actual adaptive value.

For trading, we would take an even more
conservative approach.

We'd first test regime classification offline,
then evaluate it through walk-forward and
forward validation, keeping the existing
live trading system unchanged.

The key question for us isn't whether a
regime detector looks good historically,
but whether its decisions add measurable
value on genuinely unseen data.

Thanks for the feedback. It's a useful
point for our research.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: freezing it first is what matters. the other leak is how often you go back to the unseen set: every look turns a little of it into training data, so log each evaluation and keep one slice you only open once, at the end.

replies.author: Rare_Reference3909
replies.body:
That's an excellent point.

I completely agree that repeatedly checking
the holdout can introduce indirect overfitting,
even when the model itself isn't retrained.

We've already encountered this distinction
in our forecasting research.

Once a dataset has been used to evaluate
a version, we no longer consider it
a genuinely unseen final holdout for
subsequent development.

For our future APEX-Trader research,
we want to formalize this further:

- Freeze the model, parameters and evaluation
  protocol before the final test.
- Maintain separate development and validation
  datasets.
- Record every evaluation and configuration.
- Reserve a final untouched holdout for
  one-time evaluation.

The goal is to avoid confusing repeated
experimentation with genuine out-of-sample
evidence.

Thanks again. This is exactly the kind of
methodological feedback we're looking for.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: retiring a set once it's been looked at is the habit most people skip. after it has judged one version it's validation data, not a test set, and most backtest write-ups never say which one they reported.
